title: Attention Mechanisms
oneLiner: Attention lets a model look back at every part of its input and decide, for each output, which parts matter most.

what.html:
Attention is a learned, weighted average. For each thing the model is trying to produce, it scores every input item for relevance, turns the scores into weights that add up to 1, and blends the items using those weights.

Everyday versionAnswering an exam question with an open textbook: you don't re-read the whole book or rely on a one-line memory of it. You scan the headings (keys) for what you need (your query) and read mostly from the relevant pages (values), glancing only lightly at the rest.

In the vocabulary: a query is compared with keys; the match scores become weights; the weights mix the values.

why.html:
• Translation, summarisation and question answering map one sequence to another of a different length.
  • The classic encoder–decoder squeezes the whole input into one fixed vector, so long inputs lose their beginning (quality drops beyond ~30 words).
  • Attention gives the decoder a fresh, focused summary at every step instead.
  • It's the building block of the Transformer, and so of BERT, GPT and today's large language models.

how.title: Encoder–decoder: read, then write
how.html: An encoder RNN reads the input and hands its final state (the context vector c) to a decoder RNN, which writes the output one token at a time, feeding each word back in. This decouples input and output lengths: 15 words in, "1947" out.

how.title: Practice with answers, perform without
how.html: During training the decoder is given the correct previous word (teacher forcing). At test time it must use its own guesses, which it never practised on, so one early mistake can snowball (exposure bias).

how.title: The bottleneck
how.html: Everything the encoder read must fit in one vector of, say, 512 numbers. In a long review, the early "initial impressions were good" and the late "very disappointed" get blended together; the decoder can't zoom in on the part it needs.

how.title: Attention: a fresh context at every step
how.html: Keep all encoder states. At each decoder step, score each one against what the decoder needs now, softmax the scores into weights, and take the weighted average as this step's context. Different output words get different contexts.

how.title: Three examples
how.html: Gold price: the last three days get the most weight, giving a forecast of ₹6,261. Sentiment: "excellent" gets 35% of the weight despite "slow", so the review is classified Positive. Q&A: for "What is the national capital?", "Delhi" gets 45%, "national" 20%, and "financial capital" is mostly ignored. Attention is soft pooling: between "pick the max" and "average everything", with weights the model learns.

how.title: Queries, keys and values
how.html: Think of a database: the query is your question, the keys are the index labels, the values are the stored content. Attention compares the query with every key, then returns a blend of values weighted by how well each key matched: a soft, differentiable lookup.

how.title: Scoring how well a query matches a key
how.html: Dot product: multiply and add (fast, no parameters). Additive (Bahdanau): a tiny neural network with tanh (more flexible, works when sizes differ, slower). Multiplicative (Luong): qᵀWk. Transformers use the dot product because it's one big matrix multiply on a GPU.

how.title: Why divide by √d
how.html: Dot products of long vectors get large (their spread grows like √d). Large scores push softmax to an all-or-nothing choice where gradients vanish. Dividing by √d keeps the scores in a comfortable range: scaled dot-product attention, softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V.

how.title: Bahdanau attention for translation
how.html: The 2014 breakthrough: a bidirectional encoder describes each source word in context; at each step the decoder scores every source word using its previous state, builds a context, then predicts the next word. The weights form an alignment: "kitaab" lines up with "book", "achchhi" with "good". Decode greedily or with beam search.

how.title: Self, cross, masked and multi-head
how.html: Self-attention: a sequence attends to itself ("he" finds "student"). Cross-attention: one sequence attends to another (English decoder → Hindi source). Masked: each word may only look at earlier words, as in text generation. Multi-head: several attentions in parallel, each free to track a different relationship (syntax, meaning, neighbours).

how.title: Why attention beat RNNs
how.html: In self-attention every word connects to every other word in one step, and all positions are computed at once on a GPU. An RNN must pass information along the chain step by step. The price: the attention table grows with the square of the length.

how.title: Telling the model about word order
how.html: Attention by itself ignores order: shuffle the words and each word gets the same output, just shuffled. So we add a positional encoding to each word: a pattern of sine and cosine waves at different speeds, unique for every position. Moving k steps rotates every wave by a fixed amount, so "3 words back" looks the same anywhere in the sentence.

demo.html: Three past days are the keys; the query describes tomorrow. Click on the plot to move the query and watch the weights and the blended price change. Turn up sharpness to see attention become a hard choice, or tick √d scaling to soften it. At the query, the correct weights are 0.276, 0.484, 0.240.

example.html:
Question answering: "Where is Reserve Bank?" → attention 0.55 on "Mumbai" in the context. Translation: Hindi "yah kitaab bahut achchhi hai" → "This book is very good", with a near-diagonal alignment. Forecasting: hour 24 attends to hours 17, 10 and 3 to pick up a 7-hour cycle.

Supplementary A support chatbot over network-operations manuals uses cross-attention from the user's question to retrieved document passages; inspecting the attention weights helps engineers see which paragraph the answer leaned on (with caution: weights are hints, not proofs).

misunderstandings: Attention weights tell you exactly why the model decided something.
They show where information was mixed from; they're a useful hint, not a full explanation.
It's order-blind until positional encodings are added.
In seq2seq it sits on top of encoder states; the Transformer later removed the RNN entirely.
Masked attention is only used when generating.
It's also used in training so the model can't peek at the words it must predict.
More heads always cost proportionally more.
Each head works in a smaller space (d/h), so total cost stays about the same.
takeaways: Encoder–decoder models squeeze the input into one context vector; long inputs suffer (the bottleneck).
Attention = softmax(scores) over keys, then a weighted sum of values; a fresh context at every step.
Scores: dot product, scaled dot product (÷√d_k, the Transformer default), additive (Bahdanau), multiplicative (Luong).
Self-, cross-, masked (causal) and multi-head attention serve different purposes.
Self-attention connects all positions in one step but is order-blind, so positional encodings are added.
thirty: Encoder–decoder models used to compress a whole input sentence into one fixed vector, which loses information on long inputs. Attention fixes this: at every output step, the model compares a query (what it needs now) with keys for every input position, turns the scores into weights with a softmax, and takes a weighted sum of the values. Transformers use scaled dot-product attention, softmax of Q K-transpose over root d times V. Self-attention relates positions within one sequence, cross-attention links two sequences, causal masking blocks the future for generation, and multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel. Because attention ignores order, positional encodings such as sinusoids are added to the inputs.
